THE LIGHTHOUSE KEEPER'S LAST LOG

The tide table said low water at 4:12, but the sea in Penhallow Sound had never read the tables, and so Ysolde Marrick stood on the gallery rail at half past three with a mug of tea going cold between her mittens, watching the water draw itself back from the rocks like a held breath.

She had kept the light at Carrow Skerry for thirty-one years. For the last nineteen of them the light had been automated, which meant that a small gray box in the lamp room decided when the beam turned and a cheerful man from the Northern Lights Board came out twice a year in a boat that smelled of diesel to check that the box still agreed with itself. Ysolde stayed anyway. Nobody had formally asked her to, and nobody had formally asked her to leave. The Board's paperwork described her as "resident caretaker, non-operational," a phrase she had once read aloud to the gulls and then never repeated.

This morning the paperwork was going to catch up with her. The cheerful man, whose name was Declan Oyelaran and who had a wife and a mortgage and a habit of whistling hymns when he was nervous, had telephoned the night before. The Board was selling the station. A hotel company wanted it. There would be, he said, a generous settlement, and he whistled a verse of "Eternal Father, Strong to Save" before he hung up, which told her more than the words had.

She finished the tea anyway, because cold tea was still tea, and went in to do what she had done every morning since she was twenty-six: she opened the log.

The log was not required. The gray box kept its own record in some chip she had never seen. But Ysolde's predecessor, a taciturn Orcadian named Halvard Tegg, had left her a fat green ledger with a cracked spine and an instruction written on the flyleaf in pencil: "Write what the sea did, not what you felt about it. Feelings are for letters." She had followed the first half of that advice for three decades and ignored the second only when she was alone, which was always.

She turned to the day's page. Under the date she wrote: Wind SW force 4, backing. Visibility good, six miles. Swell two feet from the west with a longer one underneath it from somewhere farther off. A trawler, the Mary Concannon, passing north at 0640, no signals. Then she sat with the pen above the paper for some time, because she had never in thirty-one years written the next thing, which was an ending.

Below her, at the foot of the tower, the sea slapped the landing steps. She heard it the way a person hears their own pulse, only when listening for it.

At eight, the boat came. It was not Declan's boat but a smaller, brighter one, and out of it climbed a young woman in a yellow jacket that had clearly never been rained on. She carried a tablet in a rubber case and she stood on the landing looking up at the tower with an expression Ysolde recognized, because she had worn it herself the first morning: the look of someone who has been told a place is small and is discovering that it is merely tall.

"Mrs. Marrick?" the woman called. "I'm Priya. From Harcourt Hospitality. Declan said it would be all right."

"Declan says a lot of things are all right," Ysolde said, but she came down the iron stair and took the line and made it fast, because you did not leave a stranger's boat swinging whatever you thought of her business.

Priya Venkataraghavan turned out to be an architect, not a salesperson, which Ysolde found harder to dislike. She had measurements to take. She had a laser device that she pointed at walls and which produced small red dots, and Ysolde followed her from the oil store to the lamp room, watching the dots slide across the whitewash like nervous insects.

"It's extraordinary," Priya said in the lamp room. The great Fresnel lens, retired in 2006 and replaced by a polycarbonate beacon the size of a bucket, still stood in its brass cradle, a beehive of glass prisms that threw the morning into a hundred small rainbows across the floor. "Do you know it weighs two tons? And it floats on a bath of mercury. Did you know that?"

"I polished it for twelve years before they took it out of service. I know exactly what it weighs, because I had to move the weights."

"Of course. Sorry." Priya lowered the laser. She was quiet for a moment and then said, in a different voice, "They're going to want to keep it. As a feature. In the lobby, or the bar. I'm told a lens like this is a selling point."

"A selling point," Ysolde said.

"I'm not going to pretend I'm sorry about the commission. It's a good project. But I grew up in Leeds, Mrs. Marrick. The sea was a rumor. I just want you to know I don't think a hotel is nothing." She said it quickly, as if she had rehearsed it on the boat and might lose her nerve.

Ysolde looked at her for long enough that the young woman shifted her feet. Then she took the green ledger from the shelf where she had left it and laid it open on the brass rail.

"Read that," she said. "Not all of it. The last week."

Priya read. Her lips moved slightly, which Ysolde liked. Wind NE force 7. Spray over the gallery at noon. Two hundred and six shearwaters on the south ledge, counted. A container ship, Hanjin something, standing too close; called the coastguard; they were polite and already knew. The light lit at 1709 by the gray box, and I watched it do it, and it did it well.

"You write about the box," Priya said, surprised.

"I write about everything the sea does. The box is part of what the sea does, now. That's the thing nobody in Declan's office understood when they made me non-operational. A lighthouse isn't a lamp. It's a person standing in the same place long enough for the place to learn her name."

"And the hotel?"

"The hotel will have a very nice lamp," Ysolde said, "and very good towels."

Priya laughed, and then, because laughing in that room felt faintly sacrilegious, stopped. She spent four hours measuring. Ysolde made her lunch, a crab sandwich, which the young woman ate standing up on the gallery with the wind snatching at her hair, saying nothing at all, which was the most intelligent thing she did all day.

When the boat left, the afternoon had gone pearl-colored and the long swell from the west had grown a little. Ysolde watched the yellow jacket shrink to a dot. Then she went back to the ledger, and under the day's entries, in the space Halvard Tegg had reserved for feelings and she had never filled, she wrote a single line.

"The place knows my name. It will have to learn another."

She closed the book, lit no lamp, and went down to the kitchen to start supper. Above her, at 1741, the gray box clicked, and the beam began its slow, indifferent, faithful turn across the water.

THE ORCHARD RECKONING

There is a particular silence that falls in an apple orchard after the last picker has gone home. It is not true silence; the wind goes on arguing with the leaves and there is always some small animal rearranging itself in the grass. But it is the silence of a place that has finished being useful for the day, and Thaddeus Boone had come to prefer it to the noise of the day's work, which had given him nothing but a bad knee and a ledger that refused to balance.

He sat on an upturned crate at the end of Row Nine with his boots off and counted bins in his head. Four hundred and twelve bins of Honeycrisp this season, against five hundred and ninety the year before. Frost in April, a hailstorm in July, and in August a man from the county who walked the property with a clipboard and the sorrowful politeness of a mortician. The bank did not care about frost.

"You're sulking in the good Cortlands," said a voice behind him.

His daughter Imogen stood at the end of the row with her arms folded, still in the canvas apron she wore for sorting. She was twenty-nine and had come home from Chicago in March ostensibly for two weeks. Seven months later, her apartment lease had lapsed and her houseplants had been given to a neighbor, and neither of them had mentioned it.

"I'm not sulking. I'm accounting."

"You're doing both. It's an old family talent." She sat down in the grass, uninvited, and plucked a windfall apple and turned it over. "This one's got a worm."

"Then eat around it."

"Dad."

"What?"

She put the apple down. For a long minute she said nothing, and he waited, because he had learned that Imogen, like the trees, would not be hurried and would punish him if he tried. Across the field a barn owl lifted off the roof of the cold store and went silently about its business.

"I got an email," she said finally. "From a company called Fennimore Growers. They do cider, mostly. Hard cider, a lot of it, for restaurants. They want to buy the fruit that doesn't make grade. The windfalls, the hail-marked ones, the ones the packers reject."

"We sell that to the juice plant."

"For nine cents a pound. They're offering twenty-two. And they'd sign a three-year contract, so the bank would see something steady." She looked at him sidelong. "I may have called them first."

Thaddeus said nothing. He was a man for whom change had always arrived as a letter from an institution, and it was strange to hear it arrive in his daughter's voice, under his own trees, smelling of cut grass and rot.

"Twenty-two cents," he said at last.

"Twenty-two."

"And what do they want from us besides apples?"

"That's the part I thought you'd hate." She took a breath. "They want us to stop spraying the lower blocks. Organic certification. It takes three years to convert, and the first two the yields drop. But the cider people pay a premium, and the premium covers it, mostly, if the winters cooperate."

"If the winters cooperate."

"I know."

The owl came back, quartering the grass at the edge of the orchard, hunting voles. Thaddeus watched it and thought about his own father, who had planted Row Nine in 1971 and who had believed, with the stubborn faith of a man who had survived a war and a lot of bad weather, that the only reliable thing on a farm was the next season. His father had sprayed whatever the extension office recommended and never once asked what it did to the owls.

"Your grandfather would have thrown you off the property."

"Maybe," Imogen said. "Or he'd have asked how many bins."

It was true, and it startled a laugh out of him, rough and rusty, the first in some weeks. He rubbed his bad knee and then, to his own surprise, held out a hand. She put the wormy apple in it. He turned it over, found the small neat hole, and bit into the other side.

"Sour," he said.

"It's a cider apple. They're supposed to be."

"Then maybe that's what the whole orchard has been trying to tell us." He chewed, considering. "Send them a reply. Tell them we'll talk. Tell them Thaddeus Boone wants to see the contract before he sees a lawyer, and he wants it in English."

"Dad, I already told them that."

"Of course you did." He shook his head slowly, and for the first time in months the ledger in his mind stopped refusing him. "Get the other crate. I'm not sitting here by myself."

She fetched it. The two of them sat in the dusk in Row Nine, a farmer and his daughter and a worm-eaten apple, while the owl worked the field and the first cold stars came out over the Cortlands.

AFTERIMAGE

The transit authority on Kepler Station had a rule that no ship carrying the dead could dock on a public berth, and so Commander Idris Okonkwo-Reyes brought the Lantern Fish in through the freight lock at the hour when the shift changed and the corridors were crowded enough that nobody looked up.

She had practice at not being looked at. Eleven years in survey service teaches you to move through a crowd like a fish through reeds. But the cargo she carried was not the kind you could hide behind a crowd, and by the time she reached Dock Nine she could feel the small hairs rise on her arms at every glance.

The cargo was one man. His name was Ansel Verhoeven, he had been a xenobiologist, and he had been dead for fourteen months, though the thing in the cryo-cradle behind her was not exactly a corpse. Seven hundred and twenty days earlier, on the ice moon Tethys-Minor, Verhoeven had walked into a cavern of luminous fungal stalks and had come out three hours later speaking in a voice that was not entirely his own. He had gone on speaking for a week. Then he had stopped, and the doctors on the survey ship had pronounced a cause of death that was a polite way of saying they did not know.

Idris had loved him, in the careful, unspoken way that people on long deployments love. And in the last hour of his life he had grasped her wrist and said, quite clearly and in his own voice, "Take me to Halloran. Tell her it's in the afterimage."

Dr. Maren Halloran received them in a laboratory so clean it had the faint smell of nothing, the way a cold room smells of cold. She was small and very upright and wore her gray hair cropped close, and she listened to Idris's account without once looking at the cradle, which Idris found she respected.

"The afterimage," Halloran said when Idris had finished. "He said it like that? That exact word?"

"Yes."

"Then I think I know what he meant. Sit down, Commander. This will take a little time, and you won't like the shape of it."

She brought up a display on the wall, a slow three-dimensional map of branching filaments, and Idris recognized the structure from the fungal cavern: the same lattice, the same pale, pulsing glow.

"You know that when you stare at a bright light and then close your eyes, you continue to see it. A ghost of the thing, printed on the retina. We call that an afterimage. What I believe the organism on Tethys-Minor does is something similar, but at the level of neural tissue. It doesn't communicate in the sense we mean. It imprints. A mind passes through, and the organism records a pattern of that mind's firing, as faithfully as a photograph, and then it plays the pattern back through whatever nervous system is nearest."

"So the voice."

"Wasn't Ansel. It was an echo of something that had passed through that cavern long before he did. Maybe thousands of years before." Halloran's voice was level, but her hands, folded in her lap, had tightened. "And then the pattern burned itself into him. His own mind started to give way to it, the way an old film gets overwritten by a new exposure."

Idris looked at the cradle for the first time since entering. The frost on its lid had begun to bead. "He said it's in the afterimage. That means there's something still there. Of him."

"That's my suspicion. If the organism recorded him as it recorded the others, there will be a residue in the tissue. Not a person. I want to be very clear about that. A pattern, a set of habits of firing. But enough, perhaps, to read."

"To read." Idris tasted the word. "And then what? You talk to it?"

"I don't know. I don't know whether what we'd find would feel anything, or whether it would be only an elaborate recording, like a letter that keeps saying the same sentence. That is the part you won't like. We would be asking a machine, essentially, to tell us whether it is a man."

The room hummed. Somewhere in the walls, a pump cycled. Idris thought of Ansel on the observation deck of the survey ship, three weeks into the deployment, arguing with her about whether the moons of Tethys were old or merely patient. He had been wrong, and delighted to be wrong, and she had thought, I will remember this forever, which was what everyone thinks and no one does.

"Do it," she said.

"Commander, you should consider—"

"I considered for fourteen months, Doctor. I did the considering at three in the morning on a ship with a body in the hold. I've run out of considering." She stood. "He asked me to bring him here. I brought him. Whatever you find, I want to be in the room."

Halloran studied her for a long moment, then nodded once, a small, formal gesture, as between two people sealing a contract.

It took nine hours. At the end of it the wall display flickered and a single line of text appeared, in the flat, unpunctuated cadence of a decoded signal, and Idris, who had braced for strangeness, found instead that it was almost unbearably ordinary.

it was cold in the cavern and I thought of you and the argument about the moons

She said nothing for a long time. Halloran, wisely, said nothing either. At length Idris reached out and laid her palm against the cold glass of the cradle, and spoke very softly, the way one speaks to a sleeper.

"Patient," she said. "You were right. They were patient."

The text on the wall did not change. It was only a recording, after all, and recordings cannot answer. But Idris stood there with her hand on the glass until the lights cycled down for the night watch, and when she finally left, she was surprised to find that she was not weeping, only lighter, as if some long-carried weight had finally been set on the ground and found to be the exact size of the hands that had held it.

THE CASE OF THE MISSING METRONOME

Inspector Hollis Tamworth-Lyle disliked cases that began with a theft of something nobody could possibly want. A diamond, yes; a diamond had a market. But a metronome?

"A Maelzel, mind you," said Mrs. Cordelia Pettigrew, who had called the constabulary at seven that morning and was now conducting the Inspector through the music room of Ashby House with the brisk proprietary air of a woman showing off a prize heifer. "Walnut case, brass weight, wound by key. Belonged to my late husband's grandfather. Valued at, oh, perhaps two hundred pounds, but of course to us it's priceless."

"Naturally," said Tamworth-Lyle, who had learned that this was a safe thing to say in almost any circumstance. "And when did you last see it?"

"Last night. Mr. Fenwick, my nephew, was practicing the Schumann. He always uses it. He is quite devoted. He put it on the piano at ten and the house was locked by eleven. This morning, gone."

The room was handsome and cold. A Broadwood grand stood under the window with its lid up. There was a pale rectangle on the polished top, a clean oblong in the thin layer of dust, where the metronome had sat. The Inspector bent, squinting. He did not touch it.

"The windows?"

"Latched. The doors locked, and I keep the keys."

"And who is in the house?"

"Myself. My nephew Fenwick. Mrs. Dunmore the cook, who sleeps in. The maid, Tilly. And Dr. Abelard Quince, my husband's physician, who has been staying while he recovers from a chest complaint." She ticked them off on her gloved fingers like items on a shopping list. "Five of us. Six, counting you."

"I would rather not be counted, madam, if it is all the same."

He interviewed them in the morning room one at a time. Fenwick Pettigrew, a pale young man with ink on his cuffs, was indignant. "Of course I didn't take it! I'd sooner steal my own hand. Without the metronome I've no idea whether I'm rushing the second movement. I rush, you see. Dreadfully." Mrs. Dunmore the cook was stout and unflappable and said she had been in the kitchen from five and would have noticed a burglar because the kitchen cat noticed everything. Tilly, the maid, was seventeen and trembling and said she hadn't been in the music room since Tuesday, not once, and there was no use asking.

"I haven't asked, Tilly," the Inspector said gently.

"No, sir. Sorry, sir."

That was the first oddity. People who have nothing to hide seldom volunteer an alibi nobody has requested. But Tamworth-Lyle filed it away and moved to the physician, who was sitting by the fire in a plaid rug, wheezing slightly, with a sheaf of medical journals open on his knees.

"A metronome," said Dr. Quince, in the tone of a man pronouncing a rare disease. "Extraordinary. Who would steal a metronome?"

"That is rather the question."

"I should think someone with an ear for rhythm and no scruples." He chuckled and coughed. "I am joking, Inspector. I was in bed at ten. I took my powder, as I do every night, and slept like the dead."

"The powder. What is it?"

"Veronal. Doctor's orders. Physician, heal thyself and so on." He smiled. "You'll find the bottle on my nightstand."

Tamworth-Lyle thanked him and returned to the music room alone. He stood for some time looking at the clean oblong in the dust. Then he did what he often did when baffled: he stopped looking at what was missing and looked instead at what was there.

On the piano's music desk lay the Schumann, open to the second movement. Over the page, in pencil, someone had marked a series of small tick marks above the bar lines, in groups of four. Nothing unusual in that. A pianist counting. But in the margin beside the final bars, in a different pencil and a different hand, a figure had been scribbled and half erased: 6 5 / 4 3 / 4.

He frowned at it. It was not a tempo marking. A tempo would read a hundred and something. It looked more like a series of numbers somebody had noted in haste.

He crouched and looked under the piano. Nothing. He ran a hand along the lower edge of the instrument's case and his finger caught on a tiny scrap of paper wedged beneath the pedal lyre. He drew it out with tweezers from his waistcoat pocket. It was a ticket, small and gray: a left-luggage receipt from the railway station at Ludlow, stamped with yesterday's date.

"Mrs. Pettigrew," he said, returning to the morning room, "does your nephew travel to Ludlow?"

"Never. Fenwick hates trains."

"Does anyone in the household?"

There was a pause that stretched slightly too long. Then Tilly, standing by the door with a tray, dropped a teacup.

It took very little after that. The girl wept and the story came out in tatters: her brother Albert, a railway porter at Ludlow, who had a debt to a bookmaker; a conversation overheard in the kitchen about the Maelzel's worth; a plan, foolish, hasty, ill-considered, to take it to the left-luggage office and let Albert sell it on. She had done it at midnight with the spare key from Mrs. Pettigrew's drawer, on her bare feet, terrified. She had dropped the ticket accidentally in the dark.

"And the numbers in the margin of the Schumann?" the Inspector asked.

"I don't know anything about numbers, sir. Honestly."

He believed her. And that, he reflected later, was the puzzle's last small joy. The numbers belonged to Fenwick, who admitted, blushing, that they were the tempo markings he had been trying out through the night: sixty-five, then sixty-four, then a hundred and forty-four. He had been experimenting, and he had indeed been rushing.

The Inspector recovered the metronome from the Ludlow left-luggage office that afternoon. It was ticking quietly in its walnut case, sitting on a shelf between a hatbox and a dead man's umbrella, set, by some accident of the porter's curiosity, to a gentle andante. Mrs. Pettigrew declined to press charges, on the condition that Tilly be given a more suitable situation, and Fenwick played the second movement of the Schumann that evening with the Maelzel at his elbow, slowly, correctly, and for the first time in recorded history not rushing at all.

TWO LINES AT THE EDGE OF THE DESERT

"You can't park here."

"I can park anywhere I like. It's a desert."

"It's a protected wash. There's a sign."

"The sign says 'Flash flood area.' There hasn't been a flood here since 1987. I looked it up." The woman in the van leaned out the window. She had sunburned shoulders, a cracked phone propped on the dashboard, and the look of someone who has been awake for a long time on principle. "Are you a ranger?"

"Volunteer. Reyes. I patrol the Nine Mile." The man in the faded green vest hooked his thumbs through his belt. He was somewhere past sixty, with a gray mustache like a tidy broom. "You're going to be trapped if it rains."

"It's not going to rain."

"It's July. It's the monsoon."

"The forecast says five percent."

"The forecast," Reyes said with feeling, "is written by a man in an air-conditioned office in Phoenix who has never in his life stood in a wash and listened to the ground."

She laughed in spite of herself. It was a short, surprised, honest laugh, and he decided he liked her slightly, which complicated his plan to be stern.

"Listen to the ground," she said. "What does that mean?"

"It means that about a half hour before the water comes there's a sound. Like a freight train a long way off. If you're lucky you hear it."

"And if you're not?"

"Then you're a news story."

She looked at the sky. It was a hard flat blue without a blemish on it. Then she looked back at him, and something in her face gave a little.

"My name is Dolores," she said. "I've been driving for nine days. I was supposed to be in Santa Fe to see my sister. She's sick. I mean she's not dying, but she's, you know." She waved a hand vaguely. "I stopped because I couldn't keep my eyes open, and there was nobody, and it was quiet. I'm sorry. I'll move."

"You don't have to apologize."

"I don't like being told what to do by strangers."

"I don't like telling anybody what to do. It's the worst part of the job." He glanced at the horizon, where a faint smudge of cloud, no larger than a thumbprint, sat low over the ridgeline. He said nothing about it. "Tell you what. There's a pullout up the road, a quarter mile, on high ground. Nobody'll bother you there. And I've got a thermos of coffee that's worse than any you've ever had."

"Is that an offer?"

"It's a warning."

Dolores started the van. In the rearview mirror the old man's figure got smaller and smaller, standing in the road with his thermos raised like a lantern, and behind him the little cloud on the ridge had begun, very slowly, to grow.

They sat at the pullout until dark, and the coffee was indeed terrible. At a quarter to nine they heard, far off, a sound like a freight train, and neither of them said anything. Then, below them, in the dark where the van had been parked, the wash filled with a low brown roar, carrying tumbleweeds and a broken fencepost and the whole astonished silence of the desert downstream.

The transit authority on Kepler Station had a rule that no ship carrying the dead could dock on a public berth, and so Commander Idris Okonkwo-Reyes brought the Lantern Fish in through the freight lock at the hour when the shift changed and the corridors were crowded enough that nobody looked up.

Idris had loved him, in the careful, unspoken way that people on long deployments love. And in the last hour of his life he had grasped her wrist and said, quite clearly and in his own voice, "Take me to Halloran. Tell her it's in the afterimage."

Dr. Maren Halloran received them in a laboratory so clean it had the faint smell of nothing, the way a cold room smells of cold. THE CASE OF THE MISSING METRONOME

Inspector Hollis Tamworth-Lyle disliked cases that began with a theft of something nobody could possibly want. A diamond, yes; a diamond had a market. But a metronome?

"A Maelzel, mind you," said Mrs. Cordelia Pettigrew, who had called the constabulary at seven that morning and was now conducting the Inspector through the music room of Ashby House with the brisk proprietary air of a woman showing off a prize heifer. "Walnut case, brass weight, wound by key. Belonged to my late husband's grandfather. Valued at, oh, perhaps two hundred pounds, but of course to us it's priceless."

"Naturally," said Tamworth-Lyle, who had learned that this was a safe thing to say in almost any circumstance. "And when did you last see it?"

"Last night. Mr. Fenwick, my nephew, was practicing the Schumann. He always uses it. He is quite devoted. He put it on the piano at ten and the house was locked by eleven. This morning, gone."

The room was handsome and cold. A Broadwood grand stood under the window with its lid up. There was a pale rectangle on the polished top, a clean oblong in the thin layer of dust, where the metronome had sat. The Inspector bent, squinting. He did not touch it.

"The windows?"

"Latched. The doors locked, and I keep the keys."

"And who is in the house?"

"Myself. My nephew Fenwick. Mrs. Dunmore the cook, who sleeps in. The maid, Tilly. And Dr. Abelard Quince, my husband's physician, who has been staying while he recovers from a chest complaint." She ticked them off on her gloved fingers like items on a shopping list. "Five of us. Six, counting you."

"I would rather not be counted, madam, if it is all the same."

He interviewed them in the morning room one at a time. Fenwick Pettigrew, a pale young man with ink on his cuffs, was indignant. "Of course I didn't take it! I'd sooner steal my own hand. Without the metronome I've no idea whether I'm rushing the second movement. I rush, you see. Dreadfully." Mrs. Dunmore the cook was stout and unflappable and said she had been in the kitchen from five and would have noticed a burglar because the kitchen cat noticed everything. Tilly, the maid, was seventeen and trembling and said she hadn't been in the music room since Tuesday, not once, and there was no use asking.

"I haven't asked, Tilly," the Inspector said gently.

"No, sir. Sorry, sir."

That was the first oddity. People who have nothing to hide seldom volunteer an alibi nobody has requested. But Tamworth-Lyle filed it away and moved to the physician, who was sitting by the fire in a plaid rug, wheezing slightly, with a sheaf of medical journals open on his knees.

"A metronome," said Dr. Quince, in the tone of a man pronouncing a rare disease. "Extraordinary. Who would steal a metronome?"

"That is rather the question."

"I should think someone with an ear for rhythm and no scruples." He chuckled and coughed. "I am joking, Inspector. I was in bed at ten. I took my powder, as I do every night, and slept like the dead."

"The powder. What is it?"

"Veronal. Doctor's orders. Physician, heal thyself and so on." He smiled. "You'll find the bottle on my nightstand."

Tamworth-Lyle thanked him and returned to the music room alone. He stood for some time looking at the clean oblong in the dust. Then he did what he often did when baffled: he stopped looking at what was missing and looked instead at what was there.

On the piano's music desk lay the Schumann, open to the second movement. Over the page, in pencil, someone had marked a series of small tick marks above the bar lines, in groups of four. Nothing unusual in that. A pianist counting. But in the margin beside the final bars, in a different pencil and a different hand, a figure had been scribbled and half erased: 6 5 / 4 3 / 4.

He frowned at it. It was not a tempo marking. A tempo would read a hundred and something. It looked more like a series of numbers somebody had noted in haste.

He crouched and looked under the piano. Nothing. He ran a hand along the lower edge of the instrument's case and his finger caught on a tiny scrap of paper wedged beneath the pedal lyre. He drew it out with tweezers from his waistcoat pocket. It was a ticket, small and gray: a left-luggage receipt from the railway station at Ludlow, stamped with yesterday's date.

"Mrs. Pettigrew," he said, returning to the morning room, "does your nephew travel to Ludlow?"

"Never. Fenwick hates trains."

"Does anyone in the household?"

There was a pause that stretched slightly too long. Then Tilly, standing by the door with a tray, dropped a teacup.

It took very little after that. The girl wept and the story came out in tatters: her brother Albert, a railway porter at Ludlow, who had a debt to a bookmaker; a conversation overheard in the kitchen about the Maelzel's worth; a plan, foolish, hasty, ill-considered, to take it to the left-luggage office and let Albert sell it on. She had done it at midnight with the spare key from Mrs. Pettigrew's drawer, on her bare feet, terrified. She had dropped the ticket accidentally in the dark.

"And the numbers in the margin of the Schumann?" the Inspector asked.

"I don't know anything about numbers, sir. Honestly."

He believed her. And that, he reflected later, was the puzzle's last small joy. The numbers belonged to Fenwick, who admitted, blushing, that they were the tempo markings he had been trying out through the night: sixty-five, then sixty-four, then a hundred and forty-four. He had been experimenting, and he had indeed been rushing.

The Inspector recovered the metronome from the Ludlow left-luggage office that afternoon. It was ticking quietly in its walnut case, sitting on a shelf between a hatbox and a dead man's umbrella, set, by some accident of the porter's curiosity, to a gentle andante. Mrs. Pettigrew declined to press charges, on the condition that Tilly be given a more suitable situation, and Fenwick played the second movement of the Schumann that evening with the Maelzel at his elbow, slowly, correctly, and for the first time in recorded history not rushing at all.

WHAT THE RIVER KEPT

My grandmother never learned to swim, and she lived beside the river for eighty-one years. When I asked her about this, the summer I was eleven, she looked at me over the rim of her enamel cup as if I had asked why she had never learned to fly.

"You do not swim in a thing you are in conversation with," she said.

The river was the Vesna, which in her village meant spring, though it was a brown, slow, thoughtful river that seemed to have given up on the season a long time ago. It ran past the back of her garden in a wide bend, and in the evenings the light came down through the willows and turned the water the color of weak tea. She had a bench there, a plank on two stumps, and she sat on it every evening with her cup and her silence and her particular way of tilting her head, as though listening for a footfall.

I was sent to her that year because my parents were not speaking to each other in the way that parents do before they stop speaking altogether. No one explained this. I was given a duffel bag, a train ticket and a stern instruction to be useful, and I arrived in a village of forty houses with the vague conviction that I had been exiled for something I had done.

My grandmother did not ask what I had done. She handed me a bucket.

The first week was all buckets. I carried water to the beans, I carried scraps to the hens, I carried a bucket of ash from the stove to the compost with such gravity that she gently took it from me and said, "It is ash, Tomas. It will not bite." In the afternoons, when the heat made the whole valley drowsy, she taught me the names of things: the heron that stood in the shallows like a bent nail, the kingfisher that was a flash of blue and nothing else, the willow-herb that grew in the ditches and turned pink in August.

On the ninth day I found the box.

It was in the crawl space under the kitchen, where I had gone looking for a lost hen. An old tin biscuit box, rusted at the hinges, wrapped in oilcloth and tied with a string that had gone stiff as wire. Inside were seven stones. They were river stones, smooth and gray, each about the size of a plum, and each had a name scratched into it with a nail. I recognized none of them. Pavel. Irena. Little Josef. Old Marta. Anton. Stefa. And one that had no name at all, only a small crooked cross.

I carried the box up into the light and set it on the kitchen table, and my grandmother, who was peeling potatoes, did not look surprised. She wiped her hands on her apron and sat down across from me.

"So," she said. "You found the river's share."

She told me the story slowly, in pieces, the way she told everything. When she was a girl, the Vesna flooded every spring, and the village lost something to it each year: a goat, a fence, a boat. Her own grandmother had begun the custom. Whenever the river took someone, a person, not a goat, the family went down to the bank at the lowest water of the following autumn and chose a stone, and wrote the name on it, and kept it. "So that the river would not be the only one remembering," she said.

"But why do you have them?"

"Because nobody else wanted them." She said it without bitterness. "People want to forget. They put them away, they say that is enough. But a name is like a seed. If you bury it, it comes up somewhere else, in some way you cannot predict. It is better to hold it where you can see it."

"Who's the one with no name?"

She was quiet for a long moment. Outside a hen was complaining and the heat pressed at the window glass.

"That one is mine," she said. "I carved the cross but I never knew what to put under it. He was a baby, Tomas. Not born long enough to be given a name. My first. The river took him in the flood of fifty-four, when the water came into the house in the night, and I was nineteen and I held him above my head until the roof gave way, and then I did not have him anymore."

I did not know what to say, and so for once I said nothing. She reached out and put her dry, strong hand on top of mine and left it there.

"This is why I do not swim," she said, very gently. "Do you understand? I do not trust myself in that water. Not because I am afraid. Because I would not come out again."

That evening we went down to the bench together. The light was coming through the willows, and the heron stood where it always stood, a bent nail against the brown, and for a while neither of us spoke. When it got dark enough that the first bats appeared, my grandmother said, "Choose a stone."

I looked at her. "For what?"

"For whatever you are carrying. You came here carrying something. I can see it the way I can see the weather on the hills. You do not have to tell me what it is. But you should put a name on it."

I went down to the water's edge, to the shallows where the pebbles gleamed in the last gray light, and picked one that fit in my palm. Then I walked back up the bank and she gave me the nail, and I sat there with it for a very long time, trying to decide what to write.

In the end I wrote only one word. It was not the name of a person. It was the name of the quiet kitchen in the apartment where my parents had stopped talking, and the dish in the sink, and the radio turned low. I wrote home, and then, underneath it, because it seemed to belong, I scratched a small crooked cross.

My grandmother nodded as if I had said something wise. "Good," she said. "Now it is in the box. And now it is something that has happened, and not something that is happening."

I have thought about that sentence for forty years. I did not understand it then. My parents divorced the following winter, and I did not weep, and I was angry at myself for not weeping, until the spring when I finally did, on a train, in front of a very surprised conductor. But in my wallet I have carried ever since a photograph of seven river stones on an oilcloth, and, behind it, a small flat gray pebble that I took from the Vesna before I left. It has no name on it. It does not need one. It is only something I carry, which is a different thing, I have learned, from something that carries me.

Inspector Hollis Tamworth-Lyle disliked cases that began with a theft of something nobody could possibly want. A diamond, yes; a diamond had a market. But a metronome?

"A Maelzel, mind you," said Mrs. Cordelia Pettigrew, who had called the constabulary at seven that morning and was now conducting the Inspector through the music room of Ashby House with the brisk proprietary air of a woman showing off a prize heifer. "Walnut case, brass weight, wound by key. Belonged to my late husband's grandfather. Valued at, oh, perhaps two hundred pounds, but of course to us it's priceless."

"Naturally," said Tamworth-Lyle, who had learned that this was a safe thing to say in almost any circumstance. "And when did you last see it?"

"Last night. Mr. Fenwick, my nephew, was practicing the Schumann. He always uses it. He is quite devoted. He put it on the piano at ten and the house was locked by eleven. This morning, gone."

The room was handsome and cold. A Broadwood grand stood under the window with its lid up. There was a pale rectangle on the polished top, a clean oblong in the thin layer of dust, where the metronome had sat. The Inspector bent, squinting. He did not touch it.

"The windows?"

"Latched. The doors locked, and I keep the keys."

"And who is in the house?"

"Myself. My nephew Fenwick. Mrs. Dunmore the cook, who sleeps in. The maid, Tilly. And Dr. Abelard Quince, my husband's physician, who has been staying while he recovers from a chest complaint." She ticked them off on her gloved fingers like items on a shopping list. "Five of us. Six, counting you."

"I would rather not be counted, madam, if it is all the same."

He interviewed them in the morning room one at a time. Fenwick Pettigrew, a pale young man with ink on his cuffs, was indignant. "Of course I didn't take it! I'd sooner steal my own hand. Without the metronome I've no idea whether I'm rushing the second movement. I rush, you see. Dreadfully." Mrs. Dunmore the cook was stout and unflappable and said she had been in the kitchen from five and would have noticed a burglar because the kitchen cat noticed everything. Tilly, the maid, was seventeen and trembling and said she hadn't been in the music room since Tuesday, not once, and there was no use asking.

"I haven't asked, Tilly," the Inspector said gently.

"No, sir. Sorry, sir."

That was the first oddity. People who have nothing to hide seldom volunteer an alibi nobody has requested. But Tamworth-Lyle filed it away and moved to the physician, who was sitting by the fire in a plaid rug, wheezing slightly, with a sheaf of medical journals open on his knees.

"A metronome," said Dr. Quince, in the tone of a man pronouncing a rare disease. "Extraordinary. Who would steal a metronome?"

"That is rather the question."

"I should think someone with an ear for rhythm and no scruples." He chuckled and coughed. "I am joking, Inspector. I was in bed at ten. I took my powder, as I do every night, and slept like the dead."

"The powder. What is it?"

"Veronal. Doctor's orders. Physician, heal thyself and so on." He smiled. "You'll find the bottle on my nightstand."

Tamworth-Lyle thanked him and returned to the music room alone. He stood for some time looking at the clean oblong in the dust. Then he did what he often did when baffled: he stopped looking at what was missing and looked instead at what was there.

On the piano's music desk lay the Schumann, open to the second movement. Over the page, in pencil, someone had marked a series of small tick marks above the bar lines, in groups of four. Nothing unusual in that. A pianist counting. But in the margin beside the final bars, in a different pencil and a different hand, a figure had been scribbled and half erased: 6 5 / 4 3 / 4.

He frowned at it. It was not a tempo marking. A tempo would read a hundred and something. It looked more like a series of numbers somebody had noted in haste.

He crouched and looked under the piano. Nothing. He ran a hand along the lower edge of the instrument's case and his finger caught on a tiny scrap of paper wedged beneath the pedal lyre. He drew it out with tweezers from his waistcoat pocket. It was a ticket, small and gray: a left-luggage receipt from the railway station at Ludlow, stamped with yesterday's date.

"Mrs. Pettigrew," he said, returning to the morning room, "does your nephew travel to Ludlow?"

"Never. Fenwick hates trains."

"Does anyone in the household?"

There was a pause that stretched slightly too long. Then Tilly, standing by the door with a tray, dropped a teacup.

It took very little after that. The girl wept and the story came out in tatters: her brother Albert, a railway porter at Ludlow, who had a debt to a bookmaker; a conversation overheard in the kitchen about the Maelzel's worth; a plan, foolish, hasty, ill-considered, to take it to the left-luggage office and let Albert sell it on. She had done it at midnight with the spare key from Mrs. Pettigrew's drawer, on her bare feet, terrified. She had dropped the ticket accidentally in the dark.

"And the numbers in the margin of the Schumann?" the Inspector asked.

"I don't know anything about numbers, sir. Honestly."

He believed her. And that, he reflected later, was the puzzle's last small joy. The numbers belonged to Fenwick, who admitted, blushing, that they were the tempo markings he had been trying out through the night: sixty-five, then sixty-four, then a hundred and forty-four. He had been experimenting, and he had indeed been rushing.

The Inspector recovered the metronome from the Ludlow left-luggage office that afternoon. It was ticking quietly in its walnut case, sitting on a shelf between a hatbox and a dead man's umbrella, set, by some accident of the porter's curiosity, to a gentle andante. Mrs. Pettigrew declined to press charges, on the condition that Tilly be given a more suitable situation, and Fenwick played the second movement of the Schumann that evening with the Maelzel at his elbow, slowly, correctly, and for the first time in recorded history not rushing at all.

TWO LINES AT THE EDGE OF THE DESERT

"You can't park here."

"I can park anywhere I like. It's a desert."

"It's a protected wash. There's a sign."

"The sign says 'Flash flood area.' There hasn't been a flood here since 1987. I looked it up." The woman in the van leaned out the window. She had sunburned shoulders, a cracked phone propped on the dashboard, and the look of someone who has been awake for a long time on principle. "Are you a ranger?"

"Volunteer. Reyes. I patrol the Nine Mile." The man in the faded green vest hooked his thumbs through his belt. He was somewhere past sixty, with a gray mustache like a tidy broom. "You're going to be trapped if it rains."

"It's not going to rain."

"It's July. It's the monsoon."

"The forecast says five percent."

"The forecast," Reyes said with feeling, "is written by a man in an air-conditioned office in Phoenix who has never in his life stood in a wash and listened to the ground."

She laughed in spite of herself. It was a short, surprised, honest laugh, and he decided he liked her slightly, which complicated his plan to be stern.

"Listen to the ground," she said. "What does that mean?"

"It means that about a half hour before the water comes there's a sound. Like a freight train a long way off. If you're lucky you hear it."

"And if you're not?"

"Then you're a news story."

She looked at the sky. It was a hard flat blue without a blemish on it. Then she looked back at him, and something in her face gave a little.

"My name is Dolores," she said. "I've been driving for nine days. I was supposed to be in Santa Fe to see my sister. She's sick. I mean she's not dying, but she's, you know." She waved a hand vaguely. "I stopped because I couldn't keep my eyes open, and there was nobody, and it was quiet. I'm sorry. I'll move."

"You don't have to apologize."

"I don't like being told what to do by strangers."

"I don't like telling anybody what to do. It's the worst part of the job." He glanced at the horizon, where a faint smudge of cloud, no larger than a thumbprint, sat low over the ridgeline. He said nothing about it. "Tell you what. There's a pullout up the road, a quarter mile, on high ground. Nobody'll bother you there. And I've got a thermos of coffee that's worse than any you've ever had."

"Is that an offer?"

"It's a warning."

Dolores started the van. In the rearview mirror the old man's figure got smaller and smaller, standing in the road with his thermos raised like a lantern, and behind him the little cloud on the ridge had begun, very slowly, to grow.

They sat at the pullout until dark, and the coffee was indeed terrible. At a quarter to nine they heard, far off, a sound like a freight train, and neither of them said anything. Then, below them, in the dark where the van had been parked, the wash filled with a low brown roar, carrying tumbleweeds and a broken fencepost and the whole astonished silence of the desert downstream.

"Huh," said Dolores.

"Yep," said Reyes.

She stayed for a second cup. In the morning, before she left, she wrote her sister's number on a napkin and gave it to him, and he gave her the thermos, and neither of them could have said why.

SCENE: THE BOARDROOM

The conference room on the fortieth floor had a view of the river and a table that seated twenty. Eight people sat at it, which made it feel emptier than it was.

"So let me see if I understand," said Gwendolyn Achterberg, the chair, tapping a pen against her tablet. "We're proposing to acquire a company that's losing eleven million a quarter, in order to save a division that's losing twelve."

"When you put it that way," said the CFO.

"Is there another way to put it?"

"There's the way where we call it a strategic realignment," said Boaz Lindqvist, from operations, and a nervous ripple went around the table.

"Boaz."

"Sorry. Yes. I'll withdraw that."

Gwendolyn set the pen down. She was sixty-three, had run the company for fourteen years, and had a reputation for asking exactly one question at each meeting that ended up being the only one that mattered. The room waited for it.

"Who," she said, "on this side of the table has actually used their product?"

Silence. A chair creaked.

"I have," said a voice from the far end, and eight heads turned. It was Nkechi, the youngest person in the room, a product analyst who had been invited only to carry the slides and who had gone quite pale. "I used it for about three weeks. In my own time. I wanted to see how the onboarding worked."

"And?"

"It's good." She swallowed. "It's really good, actually. The numbers are bad because their sales team is terrible, not because the software is. If you took the product and put it in our channel, I think customers would—" She stopped. "Sorry. It's not my place."

"It is entirely your place. You are the only person here who has used the thing." Gwendolyn turned to the CFO, an unlucky man named Pruitt. "Walt, I'd like a revised model by Friday. Assume we keep the product, drop their sales organization, and retain Ms. Okafor here as an adviser to the integration. Full salary and title. Can you do that?"

"Madam Chair, with respect, a product analyst on an integration team is—"

"Walt."

"Yes. Friday. Of course."

Nkechi sat very still. Under the table her hands were shaking. She had gone into the meeting expecting to carry slides and she was coming out of it with a career, and the sensation was exactly like stepping onto a stair that is not there.

"One more thing," said Gwendolyn, gathering her tablet. "Everyone who votes yes on this deal should use the product for one week. Not read about it. Use it. If you can't tell me what it feels like to be their customer, you have no business buying their company."

She left. The room breathed out. And Boaz Lindqvist leaned across the table toward Nkechi and whispered, with something like reverence, "You do know she's never said that to anybody before."

"Said what?"

"Your name," he said. "She remembered your name."

WHAT THE RIVER KEPT

My grandmother never learned to swim, and she lived beside the river for eighty-one years. When I asked her about this, the summer I was eleven, she looked at me over the rim of her enamel cup as if I had asked why she had never learned to fly.

"You do not swim in a thing you are in conversation with," she said.

The river was the Vesna, which in her village meant spring, though it was a brown, slow, thoughtful river that seemed to have given up on the season a long time ago. It ran past the back of her garden in a wide bend, and in the evenings the light came down through the willows and turned the water the color of weak tea. She had a bench there, a plank on two stumps, and she sat on it every evening with her cup and her silence and her particular way of tilting her head, as though listening for a footfall.

I was sent to her that year because my parents were not speaking to each other in the way that parents do before they stop speaking altogether. No one explained this. I was given a duffel bag, a train ticket and a stern instruction to be useful, and I arrived in a village of forty houses with the vague conviction that I had been exiled for something I had done.

My grandmother did not ask what I had done. She handed me a bucket.

The first week was all buckets. I carried water to the beans, I carried scraps to the hens, I carried a bucket of ash from the stove to the compost with such gravity that she gently took it from me and said, "It is ash, Tomas. It will not bite." In the afternoons, when the heat made the whole valley drowsy, she taught me the names of things: the heron that stood in the shallows like a bent nail, the kingfisher that was a flash of blue and nothing else, the willow-herb that grew in the ditches and turned pink in August.

On the ninth day I found the box.

It was in the crawl space under the kitchen, where I had gone looking for a lost hen. An old tin biscuit box, rusted at the hinges, wrapped in oilcloth and tied with a string that had gone stiff as wire. Inside were seven stones. They were river stones, smooth and gray, each about the size of a plum, and each had a name scratched into it with a nail. I recognized none of them. Pavel. Irena. Little Josef. Old Marta. Anton. Stefa. And one that had no name at all, only a small crooked cross.

I carried the box up into the light and set it on the kitchen table, and my grandmother, who was peeling potatoes, did not look surprised. She wiped her hands on her apron and sat down across from me.

"So," she said. "You found the river's share."

She told me the story slowly, in pieces, the way she told everything. When she was a girl, the Vesna flooded every spring, and the village lost something to it each year: a goat, a fence, a boat. Her own grandmother had begun the custom. Whenever the river took someone, a person, not a goat, the family went down to the bank at the lowest water of the following autumn and chose a stone, and wrote the name on it, and kept it. "So that the river would not be the only one remembering," she said.

"But why do you have them?"

"Because nobody else wanted them." She said it without bitterness. "People want to forget. They put them away, they say that is enough. But a name is like a seed. If you bury it, it comes up somewhere else, in some way you cannot predict. It is better to hold it where you can see it."

"Who's the one with no name?"

She was quiet for a long moment. Outside a hen was complaining and the heat pressed at the window glass.

"That one is mine," she said. "I carved the cross but I never knew what to put under it. He was a baby, Tomas. Not born long enough to be given a name. My first. The river took him in the flood of fifty-four, when the water came into the house in the night, and I was nineteen and I held him above my head until the roof gave way, and then I did not have him anymore."

I did not know what to say, and so for once I said nothing. She reached out and put her dry, strong hand on top of mine and left it there.

"This is why I do not swim," she said, very gently. "Do you understand? I do not trust myself in that water. Not because I am afraid. Because I would not come out again."

That evening we went down to the bench together. The light was coming through the willows, and the heron stood where it always stood, a bent nail against the brown, and for a while neither of us spoke. When it got dark enough that the first bats appeared, my grandmother said, "Choose a stone."

I looked at her. "For what?"

"For whatever you are carrying. You came here carrying something. I can see it the way I can see the weather on the hills. You do not have to tell me what it is. But you should put a name on it."

I went down to the water's edge, to the shallows where the pebbles gleamed in the last gray light, and picked one that fit in my palm. Then I walked back up the bank and she gave me the nail, and I sat there with it for a very long time, trying to decide what to write.

In the end I wrote only one word. It was not the name of a person. It was the name of the quiet kitchen in the apartment where my parents had stopped talking, and the dish in the sink, and the radio turned low. I wrote home, and then, underneath it, because it seemed to belong, I scratched a small crooked cross.

My grandmother nodded as if I had said something wise. "Good," she said. "Now it is in the box. And now it is something that has happened, and not something that is happening."

I have thought about that sentence for forty years. I did not understand it then. My parents divorced the following winter, and I did not weep, and I was angry at myself for not weeping, until the spring when I finally did, on a train, in front of a very surprised conductor. But in my wallet I have carried ever since a photograph of seven river stones on an oilcloth, and, behind it, a small flat gray pebble that I took from the Vesna before I left. It has no name on it. It does not need one. It is only something I carry, which is a different thing, I have learned, from something that carries me.

THE FOURTH ELEVATOR

Overheard in the lobby of the Meridian Tower, 5:47 p.m., Friday:

"Is that one broken?"

"That's the fourth elevator."

"I know it's the fourth elevator. There are only four. I'm asking if it's broken."

"It's not broken. It's, you know. The fourth elevator."

The first speaker, a lean man in a gray suit and a lanyard that said CONTRACTOR in blunt capitals, looked at the second, who was holding a paper coffee cup and wearing a security guard's blazer with the name tag KENNETH. Behind Kenneth the lobby stretched in marble and chrome, nearly empty at this hour. Three elevator doors stood open with the patient look of mouths about to speak. The fourth was closed, with a small laminated sign taped to the center: NOT IN SERVICE.

"So it's broken."

"Technically it's not in service."

"What's the difference?"

Kenneth sipped. He had the air of a man who had been asked this before and had once answered it, and had not enjoyed the consequences. "Broken means somebody has to fix it. Not in service means somebody decided."

"Decided what?"

"That it's not in service."

The contractor, whose name was Arjun Bhattacharya-Lowe and who had spent eleven hours wiring a data closet on the nineteenth floor, rubbed his eyes. "Kenneth. I want to go home. I have a toddler and a cat and a leak in my bathroom. I'm not looking for a philosophical discussion. Which elevators go to the garage?"

"One, two, and three."

"Then why would I take the fourth?"

"You wouldn't," said Kenneth. "That's the thing. Nobody does. It's been out since October. Management put the sign up, and then they were going to fix it, and then there was a budget thing, and then it just sort of became part of the building. Like a coat rack."

"A coat rack."

"A very large coat rack that goes up and down." Kenneth shrugged. "Sometimes at night, though, I hear it."

"Hear it."

"Going up. Past the twelfth floor, it always stops at twelve. Then I hear the doors. Then nothing. And then about forty minutes later it comes back down."

Arjun regarded him for a long moment. In the deserted lobby the air conditioning ticked. "You're telling me there's a ghost in the not-in-service elevator."

"I'm not telling you anything. I'm a security guard. I'm saying what I hear."

"Have you checked?"

"Checked what?"

"The twelfth floor. When it stops."

"I'm not paid to go to twelve, sir." Kenneth finished his coffee and crumpled the cup. "Twelve is where the accounting firm used to be, before they left. There's nothing up there. Just the carpet and the water cooler. And, to be honest, I'd like to keep it that way."

"Kenneth, you've been working this building for how long?"

"Nineteen years."

"And you've never gone up there."

"I've gone up there a hundred times, sir. Not at night. Not after the fourth elevator."

For a moment Arjun considered pressing the matter. But he was tired, and it was Friday, and the toddler was waiting. He picked up his bag and walked to elevator two, and as the doors began to close he looked back and saw the guard standing in the middle of the lobby, staring at the laminated sign with an expression that was neither fear nor longing but something quieter, the look of a man who has been keeping a secret so long it has become a friend.

On the way down, Arjun found himself humming. It took him until the garage to realize it was a hymn.

NOTES TOWARD A LETTER NEVER SENT

Dear Marguerite,

I have started this letter eleven times, and eleven times I have torn it up, and now I am doing it a twelfth time on the back of a pharmacy receipt in a train station café, because I have decided that the only way to say anything is to say it badly and fast.

I saw your mother's obituary on a website I should not have been reading. It said she had died on the fourth, peacefully, among family, and that donations could be made to the hospice instead of flowers. I read it standing in my kitchen in my socks. I read it again. And then I did what I always do, which is nothing, for three days, until I understood that nothing had become a kind of decision.

I do not know if you remember the summer of the broken dishwasher. You must; it is one of the family stories. Your mother stood in the doorway in a flowered apron with her hands on her hips and said, "Eighteen years of marriage and I'm washing plates like a peasant," and your father, God rest him, said, "Peasants wash them better." And she threw the dish towel at him. And he caught it. And all of us, you and I and the cousins, sat on the porch steps pretending not to hear and laughing into our knees.

I think of that evening more than I think of most of my wedding. There was something in how easily they fought, how safe the fighting was. It never occurred to me until years later that I had never seen anyone in my own house fight like that, in a way that was clearly another form of love.

I am sorry that I stopped writing. I would like to pretend there was a reason. There was only the ordinary drift, the missed birthday, the unreturned call, the way a rope that is not tied fraying, one thread at a time, until suddenly you are looking at the other bank and there is no bridge.

Your mother taught me to make pierogi when I was nineteen and homesick. She said the secret was that the dough had to be rested, and that most things in life were the same: they needed to be left alone for a while before they were ready to be shaped. I have made them every Christmas since. They are never as good as hers. The filling is too dry, or the edges do not seal, and every time I curse a little and think of her, in her flowered apron, saying, "Rest it, rest it, you impatient child."

I do not expect you to forgive me. I do not even know if I am asking. I think what I am saying is that I am still here, and so are the dishes, and so is the memory of the porch steps, and that if you ever want to stand in a doorway and throw a towel at someone, I would be glad to be caught off guard.

The train is called. I will leave this on the café table or put it in the post, I am not sure which. I will decide at the platform.

With love, and with a dry filling,
Helena

(The letter was found by a cleaner at 6:20 the following morning, folded in thirds under a saucer. It had no stamp and no address. The cleaner, a woman named Bernadette who read slowly, finished it standing beside the espresso machine and then, without quite knowing why, put it in her apron pocket. She did not think about it again until three weeks later, when her own sister called after nine years of silence, and she found, to her surprise, that she knew exactly what to say.)

Odalys stood under the plastic shelter with her suitcase between her feet and a paper bag of chestnuts going cold in her hand, and across the road a man in an orange coat was also waiting, and neither of them was willing to admit it.

It was the last bus. Everyone knew that. After it came nothing until six the next morning, and the nearest hotel was fourteen miles away in a town whose name she had never learned to pronounce. So she waited, and the man waited, and the wind came down off the fields carrying the smell of wet earth and distant woodsmoke.

"You can share the shelter," she called at last. "It's got a roof. Mostly."

He crossed the road with the unhurried gait of a man who had never been in a hurry in his life and stood at the opposite end of the bench. He was perhaps seventy. He carried a violin case, battered, held together at one corner with silver tape.

"Chestnut?" Odalys offered.

"Thank you. I haven't had one in years." He cracked it with his thumbnail and ate it with solemn attention. "My wife used to roast them on the stove. She burned half of them. I preferred the burned ones."

"Used to."

"Yes." He nodded. "Eleven months in March."

She did not say she was sorry, because she was tired of hearing the word herself. Instead she asked, "What do you play?"

"Whatever's asked. Weddings, mostly. Funerals, when there's no organist. Once a very strange birthday for a parrot." He tapped the case. "Tonight there was a christening in Ashgrove. The baby slept through the whole of the Bach. A critic, you see. Unimpressed."

She smiled. The wind picked up and she pulled her scarf closer, and he looked at it, a green wool thing with a loose thread at one end, and said, "That is a good scarf."

"My sister knitted it. She's terrible at it. This is the fourth attempt." Odalys turned the loose thread between her fingers. "I'm going to her now. Wendover. She just had twins and she says she needs somebody to hold things. I think she means her sanity."

"Twins," said the old man. "That is a great deal of crying."

"Is it?"

"I raised three. I recommend earplugs and a very patient dog."

They fell silent. A single headlight appeared far down the road, wavered, and turned out to be a tractor. Odalys felt a small absurd pang. She had counted on the bus the way you count on a ceiling.

"Do you know," the violinist said after a while, "I think I would like to play something."

"Here?"

"Why not? There is no one to disturb. Only a hedgehog or two."

He opened the case with the careful, tender hands of a man handling something asleep. The violin was old and dark and slightly scarred, and when he tucked it under his chin the shelter seemed to grow smaller and warmer. He tuned for a moment, a few long, aching fifths, and then he played.

It was not anything she knew. It was slow and plain, a little like a lullaby, a little like a song somebody sings alone in a kitchen. Odalys closed her eyes. The wind seemed to hold its breath. Across the dark fields a single window went gold in a farmhouse, and she thought, absurdly, that it was listening.

"""Data models for a small warehouse inventory tracker.

The models are deliberately plain dataclasses so they can be serialized to
JSON without any extra machinery. Quantities are integers (units on hand);
prices are stored in integer cents to avoid floating point surprises.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import datetime as dt
import json
from dataclasses import dataclass, field, asdict
from typing import Dict, Iterable, List, Optional


class InventoryError(Exception):
    """Base class for all errors raised by this package."""


class InsufficientStock(InventoryError):
    def __init__(self, sku: str, wanted: int, available: int) -> None:
        super().__init__(
            f"cannot remove {wanted} of {sku}: only {available} on hand"
        )
        self.sku = sku
        self.wanted = wanted
        self.available = available


@dataclass
class Item:
    sku: str
    name: str
    price_cents: int
    quantity: int = 0
    reorder_level: int = 5
    tags: List[str] = field(default_factory=list)

    def __post_init__(self) -> None:
        if self.price_cents < 0:
            raise ValueError("price_cents must be non-negative")
        if self.quantity < 0:
            raise ValueError("quantity must be non-negative")
        self.sku = self.sku.strip().upper()

    @property
    def price(self) -> float:
        return self.price_cents / 100.0

    @property
    def needs_reorder(self) -> bool:
        return self.quantity <= self.reorder_level

    def total_value_cents(self) -> int:
        return self.price_cents * self.quantity


@dataclass
class Movement:
    """A single change to stock levels, kept for auditing."""

    sku: str
    delta: int
    reason: str
    timestamp: dt.datetime = field(default_factory=dt.datetime.utcnow)

    def to_dict(self) -> dict:
        d = asdict(self)
        d["timestamp"] = self.timestamp.isoformat(timespec="seconds")
        return d


class Inventory:
    """In-memory collection of items with an append-only movement log."""

    def __init__(self, items: Optional[Iterable[Item]] = None) -> None:
        self._items: Dict[str, Item] = {}
        self._log: List[Movement] = []
        for item in items or ():
            self.add_item(item)

    # -- basic access -------------------------------------------------------

    def __len__(self) -> int:
        return len(self._items)

    def __contains__(self, sku: str) -> bool:
        return sku.strip().upper() in self._items

    def get(self, sku: str) -> Item:
        try:
            return self._items[sku.strip().upper()]
        except KeyError:
            raise InventoryError(f"unknown sku: {sku!r}") from None

    def add_item(self, item: Item) -> None:
        if item.sku in self._items:
            raise InventoryError(f"duplicate sku: {item.sku}")
        self._items[item.sku] = item
        if item.quantity:
            self._log.append(Movement(item.sku, item.quantity, "initial"))

    # -- stock changes --------------------------------------------------------

    def receive(self, sku: str, count: int, reason: str = "receipt") -> int:
        if count <= 0:
            raise ValueError("count must be positive")
        item = self.get(sku)
        item.quantity += count
        self._log.append(Movement(item.sku, count, reason))
        return item.quantity

    def remove(self, sku: str, count: int, reason: str = "shipment") -> int:
        if count <= 0:
            raise ValueError("count must be positive")
        item = self.get(sku)
        if item.quantity < count:
            raise InsufficientStock(item.sku, count, item.quantity)
        item.quantity -= count
        self._log.append(Movement(item.sku, -count, reason))
        return item.quantity

    # -- reporting ------------------------------------------------------------

    def low_stock(self) -> List[Item]:
        return sorted(
            (i for i in self._items.values() if i.needs_reorder),
            key=lambda i: (i.quantity - i.reorder_level, i.sku),
        )

    def total_value_cents(self) -> int:
        return sum(i.total_value_cents() for i in self._items.values())

    def by_tag(self, tag: str) -> List[Item]:
        return [i for i in self._items.values() if tag in i.tags]

    def history(self, sku: Optional[str] = None) -> List[Movement]:
        if sku is None:
            return list(self._log)
        key = sku.strip().upper()
        return [m for m in self._log if m.sku == key]

    # -- persistence ----------------------------------------------------------

    def to_json(self) -> str:
        payload = {
            "items": [asdict(i) for i in self._items.values()],
            "log": [m.to_dict() for m in self._log],
        }
        return json.dumps(payload, indent=2, sort_keys=True)

    @classmethod
    def from_json(cls, text: str) -> "Inventory":
        data = json.loads(text)
        inv = cls()
        for raw in data.get("items", []):
            inv._items[raw["sku"]] = Item(**raw)
        for raw in data.get("log", []):
            ts = dt.datetime.fromisoformat(raw.pop("timestamp"))
            inv._log.append(Movement(timestamp=ts, **raw))
        return inv

"""Data models for a small warehouse inventory tracker.

The models are deliberately plain dataclasses so they can be serialized to
JSON without any extra machinery. Quantities are integers (units on hand);
prices are stored in integer cents to avoid floating point surprises.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import datetime as dt
import json
from dataclasses import dataclass, field, asdict
from typing import Dict, Iterable, List, Optional


class InventoryError(Exception):
    """Base class for all errors raised by this package."""


class InsufficientStock(InventoryError):
    def __init__(self, sku: str, wanted: int, available: int) -> None:
        super().__init__(
            f"cannot remove {wanted} of {sku}: only {available} on hand"
        )
        self.sku = sku
        self.wanted = wanted
        self.available = available


@dataclass
class Item:
    sku: str
    name: str
    price_cents: int
    quantity: int = 0
    reorder_level: int = 5
    tags: List[str] = field(default_factory=list)

    def __post_init__(self) -> None:
        if self.price_cents < 0:
            raise ValueError("price_cents must be non-negative")
        if self.quantity < 0:
            raise ValueError("quantity must be non-negative")
        self.sku = self.sku.strip().upper()

    @property
    def price(self) -> float:
        return self.price_cents / 100.0

    @property
    def needs_reorder(self) -> bool:
        return self.quantity <= self.reorder_level

    def total_value_cents(self) -> int:
        return self.price_cents * self.quantity


@dataclass
class Movement:
    """A single change to stock levels, kept for auditing."""

    sku: str
    delta: int
    reason: str
    timestamp: dt.datetime = field(default_factory=dt.datetime.utcnow)

    def to_dict(self) -> dict:
        d = asdict(self)
        d["timestamp"] = self.timestamp.isoformat(timespec="seconds")
        return d


class Inventory:
    """In-memory collection of items with an append-only movement log."""

    def __init__(self, items: Optional[Iterable[Item]] = None) -> None:
        self._items: Dict[str, Item] = {}
        self._log: List[Movement] = []
        for item in items or ():
            self.add_item(item)

    # -- basic access -------------------------------------------------------

    def __len__(self) -> int:
        return len(self._items)

    def __contains__(self, sku: str) -> bool:
        return sku.strip().upper() in self._items

    def get(self, sku: str) -> Item:
        try:
            return self._items[sku.strip().upper()]
        except KeyError:
            raise InventoryError(f"unknown sku: {sku!r}") from None

    def add_item(self, item: Item) -> None:
        if item.sku in self._items:
            raise InventoryError(f"duplicate sku: {item.sku}")
        self._items[item.sku] = item
        if item.quantity:
            self._log.append(Movement(item.sku, item.quantity, "initial"))

    # -- stock changes --------------------------------------------------------

    def receive(self, sku: str, count: int, reason: str = "receipt") -> int:
        if count <= 0:
            raise ValueError("count must be positive")
        item = self.get(sku)
        item.quantity += count
        self._log.append(Movement(item.sku, count, reason))
        return item.quantity

    def remove(self, sku: str, count: int, reason: str = "shipment") -> int:
        if count <= 0:
            raise ValueError("count must be positive")
        item = self.get(sku)
        if item.quantity < count:
            raise InsufficientStock(item.sku, count, item.quantity)
        item.quantity -= count
        self._log.append(Movement(item.sku, -count, reason))
        return item.quantity

    # -- reporting ------------------------------------------------------------

    def low_stock(self) -> List[Item]:
        return sorted(
            (i for i in self._items.values() if i.needs_reorder),
            key=lambda i: (i.quantity - i.reorder_level, i.sku),
        )

    def total_value_cents(self) -> int:
        return sum(i.total_value_cents() for i in self._items.values())

    def by_tag(self, tag: str) -> List[Item]:
        return [i for i in self._items.values() if tag in i.tags]

    def history(self, sku: Optional[str] = None) -> List[Movement]:
        if sku is None:
            return list(self._log)
        key = sku.strip().upper()
        return [m for m in self._log if m.sku == key]

    # -- persistence ----------------------------------------------------------

    def to_json(self) -> str:
        payload = {
            "items": [asdict(i) for i in self._items.values()],
            "log": [m.to_dict() for m in self._log],
        }
        return json.dumps(payload, indent=2, sort_keys=True)

    @classmethod
    def from_json(cls, text: str) -> "Inventory":
        data = json.loads(text)
        inv = cls()
        for raw in data.get("items", []):
            inv._items[raw["sku"]] = Item(**raw)
        for raw in data.get("log", []):
            ts = dt.datetime.fromisoformat(raw.pop("timestamp"))
            inv._log.append(Movement(timestamp=ts, **raw))
        return inv

    return Inventory.from_json(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))

    if not items:

        return
    width = max(len(i.name) for i in items)
    print(f"{'SKU':<12} {'NAME':<{width}} {'QTY':>6} {'PRICE':>10}", file=out)
    for i in items:
        print(
            f"{i.sku:<12} {i.name:<{width}} {i.quantity:>6} "
            f"{format_money(i.price_cents):>10}",
            file=out,
        )


def print_csv(items: List[Item], out=sys.stdout) -> None:
    writer = csv.writer(out)
    writer.writerow(["sku", "name", "quantity", "price_cents"])
    for i in items:
        writer.writerow([i.sku, i.name, i.quantity, i.price_cents])

    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="inventory", description=__doc__.split("\n")[0])
    p.add_argument("--file", type=Path, default=Path("stock.json"),
                   help="path to the JSON data file (default: %(default)s)")
    sub = p.add_subparsers(dest="command", required=True)

    sub.add_parser("list", help="show every item")

    add = sub.add_parser("add", help="create a new item")
    add.add_argument("sku")
    add.add_argument("name")
    add.add_argument("price", type=float, help="unit price in dollars")
    add.add_argument("--qty", type=int, default=0)
    add.add_argument("--reorder", type=int, default=5)

    rec = sub.add_parser("receive", help="add stock")
    rec.add_argument("sku")
    rec.add_argument("count", type=int)

    ship = sub.add_parser("ship", help="remove stock")
    ship.add_argument("sku")
    ship.add_argument("count", type=int)

    low = sub.add_parser("low", help="items at or below reorder level")
    low.add_argument("--format", choices=("table", "csv"), default="table")

    sub.add_parser("value", help="total value of stock on hand")
    return p

    args = build_parser().parse_args(argv)

        elif args.command == "add":
            cents = round(args.price * 100)
            inv.add_item(Item(args.sku, args.name, cents, args.qty, args.reorder))
            save(inv, args.file)
        elif args.command == "receive":
            new_qty = inv.receive(args.sku, args.count)

    return 0
